scenes.visual: Title card 'Copy First, Then Share' over a knee with a small scrape, drawn as a flat cartoon. COLOUR MAP (both films): chromosomes RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW, each one thin thread before copying, two thin joined threads after copying in interphase, and a thick compact X only once coiled (prophase onward); cell membrane soft PEACH outline, nucleus pale GREY circle, plant cell wall DARK GREEN box outline; two on-screen counters top right, white text on charcoal: 'chromosomes: N' and 'copies: N'. All cells are cartoons labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Scrape your knee, and new skin often covers the spot in about one to two weeks. Where did those new skin cells come from?
scenes.caption: Scrape your knee, and new skin often covers the spot in about 1 to 2 weeks. Where did those new skin cells come from?
scenes.visual: Cartoon knee; a red scrape. A calendar strip along the bottom flips pages, label '1 to 2 weeks'; the scrape shrinks as pink skin closes over it.
scenes.narration: Scrape your knee, and new skin often covers the spot in about 1 to 2 weeks. Where did those new skin cells come from?

scenes.tts: Zoom in on the edge of the scrape. Skin cells near the gap divide, and each one becomes two. Some cells also crawl into the gap. Every new cell comes from a cell that was already there.
scenes.visual: Zoom to a side view: a row of PEACH skin cells with a gap in the middle. Cells two or three rows back split, one into two, with a soft pop; a few cells at the gap edge stretch and slide forward. The gap narrows while the narrator speaks. Labels 'divide' (back) and 'crawl in' (front).
scenes.narration: Zoom in on the edge of the scrape. Skin cells near the gap divide, and each one becomes two. Some cells also crawl into the gap. Every new cell comes from a cell that was already there.

scenes.tts: Here is the harder question. Most cells carry a full set of instructions. When one cell becomes two, how does each new cell get a complete set?
scenes.visual: One dividing cell is pulled out and enlarged at centre. A question mark sits above it; two empty outlines of daughter cells appear beside it, each with a dashed box labelled 'full set?'.
scenes.narration: Here is the harder question. Most cells carry a full set of instructions. When one cell becomes two, how does each new cell get a complete set?

scenes.tts: The instructions sit on chromosomes. These are threads inside the nucleus that carry the cell's instructions. Our model cell has four of them: red, blue, green and yellow.
scenes.visual: Camera moves into the nucleus. Four thin rods drift into view, coloured RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW. Counters appear: 'chromosomes: 4', 'copies: 4'. Small side note: 'a typical human body cell: 46'.
scenes.narration: The instructions sit on chromosomes. These are threads inside the nucleus that carry the cell's instructions. Our model cell has four of them: red, blue, green and yellow.

scenes.tts: A dividing cell goes through the cell cycle. It has two main parts. Interphase comes first. Then comes mitosis, when the cell divides into two new cells.
scenes.visual: A circular arrow draws itself around the cell. One arc labelled 'interphase', a second arc labelled 'mitosis'. A marker dot starts moving along the interphase arc. Arc lengths are not to scale; label 'schematic, not to scale'.
scenes.narration: A dividing cell goes through the cell cycle. It has two main parts. Interphase comes first. Then comes mitosis, when the cell divides into two new cells.

scenes.tts: In interphase the cell is busy, not resting. It grows bigger. And it copies every one of its chromosomes. Each thread gets a matching copy, joined to it. Both stay thin and spread out for now.
scenes.visual: The cell outline swells. Each coloured thread doubles alongside itself into two thin threads joined at one point, one colour at a time: RED, then BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW. The threads stay thin and loose; no compact X yet. The 'chromosomes' counter stays at 4 and is frozen with a small question mark beside it; the 'copies' counter is hidden behind a card.
scenes.narration: In interphase the cell is busy, not resting. It grows bigger. And it copies every one of its chromosomes. Each thread gets a matching copy, joined to it. Both stay thin and spread out for now.

scenes.tts: Look at the counter. Before copying, the cell had four chromosomes. Now each one is a pair of joined copies. Does the cell have four chromosomes, or eight?
scenes.visual: Pause card slides in: 'After copying: 4 chromosomes or 8?' The four pairs of thin joined threads glow softly in the nucleus.
scenes.narration: Look at the counter. Before copying, the cell had four chromosomes. Now each one is a pair of joined copies. Does the cell have four chromosomes, or eight?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer fills at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Four. A copied chromosome is still one chromosome. It is made of two identical copies, joined together. So the cell has four chromosomes, and eight copies.
scenes.visual: Card lifts. Counters flip: 'chromosomes: 4', 'copies: 8'. The RED pair zooms up; each of its two whole threads is labelled 'copy' (not its arms), and a bracket around the joined pair reads 'one chromosome'.
scenes.narration: Four. A copied chromosome is still one chromosome. It is made of two identical copies, joined together. So the cell has four chromosomes, and eight copies.

scenes.tts: Now mitosis begins. Its four stages always come in the same order. In prophase, the chromosomes coil up. Each pair of copies becomes a thick X you can see.
scenes.visual: A strip of four empty boxes along the bottom labelled 'prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase'; the first box lights. The view zooms in so the chromosomes fill the frame (no nucleus outline is drawn during mitosis); each pair of thin joined threads coils tighter and thickens into a short, bold X, still scattered, not in a row.
scenes.narration: Now mitosis begins. Its four stages always come in the same order. In prophase, the chromosomes coil up. Each pair of copies becomes a thick X you can see.

scenes.tts: In metaphase, the chromosomes line up in a row across the middle of the cell. Red, blue, green and yellow, side by side.
scenes.visual: Second box lights. The four Xs glide to a dashed line across the cell's middle and settle in a vertical row, RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW.
scenes.narration: In metaphase, the chromosomes line up in a row across the middle of the cell. Red, blue, green and yellow, side by side.

scenes.tts: In anaphase, the two copies of each chromosome are pulled apart. One copy of each colour moves to each end of the cell.
scenes.visual: Third box lights. Each X splits at its middle; one whole copy of each colour slides left, the matching copy slides right. Four single rods, one of each colour, gather at each end. The counters fade out during the move.
scenes.narration: In anaphase, the two copies of each chromosome are pulled apart. One copy of each colour moves to each end of the cell.

scenes.tts: In telophase, two new nuclei form. Then the cell splits into two. Each new cell is called a daughter cell.
scenes.visual: Fourth box lights. A pale GREY nucleus circle forms around each group of four rods. The PEACH outline pinches in at the middle and separates into two smaller round cells, each labelled 'daughter cell'.
scenes.narration: In telophase, two new nuclei form. Then the cell splits into two. Each new cell is called a daughter cell.

scenes.tts: Now count each daughter cell. Red, blue, green, yellow. Four chromosomes, one of each. That is the same set as the parent cell.
scenes.visual: Each daughter cell gets its own counter: 'chromosomes: 4'. A tick appears next to each colour in turn in both cells, one RED, one BLUE, one GREEN, one YELLOW. A faded copy of the parent cell sits above with its own '4', and an equals sign links them.
scenes.narration: Now count each daughter cell. Red, blue, green, yellow. Four chromosomes, one of each. That is the same set as the parent cell.

scenes.tts: So here is the answer to our question. Copy first, then share. Copying makes two joined copies of every chromosome. Sharing sends one copy of each to each new cell. Nothing is missing.
scenes.visual: Split screen replay at double speed: left half each thread gains a joined copy (label 'copy first'); right half the Xs split and one of each colour goes to each daughter cell (label 'then share').
scenes.narration: So here is the answer to our question. Copy first, then share. Copying makes two joined copies of every chromosome. Sharing sends one copy of each to each new cell. Nothing is missing.

scenes.tts: This is how body cells divide when you grow or when a scrape heals. Mistakes can happen. But normal division gives each new cell a full set.
scenes.visual: Pull back out through the skin cell to the healing knee, now covered with new pink skin. Small note in the corner: 'normal division; mistakes can happen'.
scenes.narration: This is how body cells divide when you grow or when a scrape heals. Mistakes can happen. But normal division gives each new cell a full set.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex holding two identical coloured sets of four chromosomes. Line: 'Copy first, then share: each new cell gets one of each.'
